specPoints.text: practical: investigate the speed of sound in air

primer.text: This core practical measures the speed of sound in air twice: once with a stopwatch over a long measured distance, and once with two microphones and an oscilloscope over a short one. Comparing the methods is where the evaluation marks live, because one of them is fighting human reaction time.

lessons.title: Timing sound over a measured distance
sourceHeadings: Experiment 1: measuring the speed of sound between two points
Measuring the speed of sound in air
lessons.opening: The oldest way to catch the speed of sound is also the simplest: make a sharp bang a known distance away, start a stopwatch when you see the bang and stop it when the sound reaches you. Distance divided by time then gives a value close to the accepted 340 m/s.
keyPoints: The experiment measures how fast sound crosses a known gap between two people.
A trundle wheel measures a distance of about 100 m between two people.
One person bangs two wooden blocks together; the other starts a stopwatch on seeing the bang and stops it on hearing it.
The timing is repeated several times and averaged, then repeated at several distances.
Speed is calculated from distance divided by time, giving about 340 m/s in air.

low.restatement: Two people stand a known distance apart, one bangs blocks while the other times the gap between seeing the bang and hearing it, and distance divided by the average time gives the speed of sound.
low.analogy: Timing a storm: you already use light as the instant signal and sound as the delayed one, so thunder counting is this experiment outdoors.
low.examPointer: Name the measuring instruments and their jobs: trundle wheel for distance, stopwatch for time, wooden blocks for the bang.

medium.restatement: Over a 100 m gap the sound takes about 0.3 s, so the stopwatch reading is largely reaction time; averaging and long distances keep the ratio usable, and distance divided by average time still lands near 340 m/s.
medium.analogy: Measuring a river by floating a stick between two bridges: a crude timing over a long baseline still reveals the speed.
medium.examPointer: If asked to improve accuracy, move the analysis onto a graph: the gradient of distance against average time cancels a constant reaction offset.

check.stem: Which instrument measures the distance travelled by the sound in experiment 1?

options.text: a stopwatch
options.explanation: A stopwatch measures time, not distance.

options.text: a trundle wheel
options.explanation: The trundle wheel rolls out distances such as the 100 m gap.

options.text: an oscilloscope
options.explanation: The oscilloscope belongs to the electronic method of experiment 2.

options.text: a wooden block
options.explanation: Blocks make the bang; they measure nothing.

check.stem: Why does the timer start the stopwatch when the blocks are seen to clash, not when they are heard?

options.text: because light travels much faster than sound, so the sight of the bang is effectively instant
options.explanation: Light reaches the timer in a negligible time compared with the sound delay.

options.text: because sound cannot travel more than 100 m
options.explanation: Sound travels any distance; it simply takes time.

options.text: because the stopwatch only responds to light
options.explanation: Stopwatches respond to fingers, not light.

options.text: because the bang is too quiet to hear
options.explanation: The bang is the very signal being timed.

check.stem: Why is the timing repeated several times and an average taken?

options.text: to make the bang louder
options.explanation: Averaging cannot change loudness.

options.text: to reduce the effect of random human reaction-time errors
options.explanation: Reaction time varies trial to trial; averaging smooths those random errors.

options.text: to increase the distance the sound travels
options.explanation: Distance is fixed by the measurement, not the repeats.

options.text: to calibrate the stopwatch against the trundle wheel
options.explanation: No calibration between instruments happens here.

check.stem: The experiment is repeated at 120 m, 140 m, 160 m and 180 m. What does plotting distance against average time allow?

options.text: the gradient of the line gives the speed of sound
options.explanation: Speed is distance over time, which is exactly the gradient of a distance-time graph.

options.text: the area under the line gives the speed of sound
options.explanation: Area has no meaning for a distance-time plot here.

options.text: the intercept gives the speed of sound
options.explanation: The intercept is the zero-distance point, not a speed.

options.text: the spread of times to be ignored
options.explanation: Plotting does not remove scatter; it exposes it.

check.stem: A group measures 180 m between the two points and records an average time of 0.53 s. What speed of sound does this give?

options.text: about 340 m/s
options.explanation: 180 / 0.53 is about 340 m/s, matching the accepted value.

options.text: about 95 m/s
options.explanation: 0.53 / 180 would mix up numerator and denominator.

options.text: about 940 m/s
options.explanation: This is nearly three times too large for air.

options.text: about 53 m/s
options.explanation: This drops the factor of ten and the division.

check.stem: State the independent and dependent variables of experiment 1.
check.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the distance between the two points and the dependent variable is the time taken for the sound to travel that distance.

check.stem: State the equation used in the analysis of the results.
check.modelAnswer: Average speed = distance moved divided by time taken.

check.stem: Explain why the stopwatch method gives a less accurate value than the oscilloscope method.
check.modelAnswer: A human timer must react to seeing and hearing events, and that reaction time is comparable with the travel time of the sound, so the recorded time carries a large random error; the oscilloscope method times the wave electronically, which removes the human reaction delay.

check.stem: A student suggests timing the bang over a gap of only 2 m with the stopwatch method. Explain whether this is sensible.
check.modelAnswer: It is not sensible: at about 340 m/s the sound crosses 2 m in roughly 0.006 s, far shorter than any human reaction time, so the stopwatch reading would be almost entirely reaction error; a larger distance makes the travel time comparable with but greater than the reaction uncertainty.

lessons.title: Timing sound with microphones and an oscilloscope
sourceHeadings: Measuring the speed of sound with an oscilloscope
lessons.opening: The electronic upgrade swaps the stopwatch for an oscilloscope: two microphones a couple of metres apart feed the scope, the bang produces one pulse on each trace, and the delay between the pulses is the travel time across the measured gap. Electronic triggering removes the reaction-time error that limits the manual method.
keyPoints: Two microphones are connected to one oscilloscope and placed a measured distance apart, about 2 m.
The oscilloscope triggers when the first microphone detects the bang.
The second microphone receives the bang later, so the traces are separated by the travel time across the gap.
A tape measure gives the microphone separation and the delay is read from the scope.
Electronic timing removes human reaction time, so the result is more precise than the stopwatch method.

low.restatement: Two microphones feed one oscilloscope; the bang shows on both traces, and the horizontal offset between the pulses divided into the known microphone separation gives the speed of sound.
low.analogy: Two runners crossing the same finish line at different times: the oscilloscope is the photo-finish camera for the sound pulse.
low.examPointer: Evaluation marks live in the comparison: name human reaction time as the weakness of method 1 and electronic triggering as the fix.

medium.restatement: The scope draws both microphone traces on one time axis; the offset in divisions converts to seconds through the time-base scale, and dividing the known separation by that delay yields the speed with no human timing in the loop.
medium.analogy: A photo-finish camera: two runners cross the same line, and the timestamp difference is the time of flight.
medium.examPointer: Evaluation pairs: reaction time (method 1’s flaw) against electronic triggering (method 2’s fix); quote both to earn the comparison marks.

check.stem: In the oscilloscope method, what triggers the oscilloscope?

options.text: the second microphone detecting the bang
options.explanation: The scope triggers on the FIRST microphone.

options.text: the first microphone detecting the bang
options.explanation: The scope is set to trigger when the first microphone receives the bang.

options.text: the wooden blocks directly
options.explanation: Blocks make sound; they are not connected to the scope.

options.text: the tape measure
options.explanation: The tape measure only fixes the separation.

check.stem: What does the horizontal separation of the two pulses on the screen represent?

options.text: the distance between the microphones
options.explanation: Distance is measured externally with the tape measure.

options.text: the time for the sound to travel from one microphone to the other
options.explanation: The trace offset is the travel time across the gap.

options.text: the amplitude of the bang
options.explanation: Amplitude is the vertical height of the trace.

options.text: the frequency of the bang
options.explanation: A single bang is a pulse, not a repeated wave.

check.stem: Which control variable is specific to the oscilloscope method?

options.text: using the same pair of microphones for every trial
options.explanation: The method declares the same set of microphones as a control variable.

options.text: banging the blocks harder each time
options.explanation: That changes conditions rather than controlling them.

options.text: moving the microphones closer each trial
options.explanation: That changes the independent variable.

options.text: using a different oscilloscope each trial
options.explanation: Equipment is kept the same, not varied.

check.stem: Why is a tape measure used rather than the trundle wheel in the oscilloscope method?

options.text: the separation is small, about 2 m, so a tape measure gives the finer resolution needed
options.explanation: A 2 m gap needs fine measurement; the tape resolution suits it.

options.text: a trundle wheel cannot measure any distance
options.explanation: A trundle wheel measures distance; it is just coarse for 2 m.

options.text: the trundle wheel only works outdoors
options.explanation: Nothing restricts the trundle wheel to outdoors.

options.text: the tape measure times the pulse as well
options.explanation: The tape measures distance only.

check.stem: Which verdict fairly compares the stopwatch timing with the oscilloscope timing?

options.text: both methods are equally accurate
options.explanation: The electronic method removes the dominant error source.

options.text: the oscilloscope method is better because electronic timing removes human reaction time
options.explanation: Reaction time is the manual method’s weakness and the electronic method removes it.

options.text: the stopwatch method is better because it uses no electricity
options.explanation: Power source is irrelevant to accuracy here.

options.text: neither method can measure the speed of sound
options.explanation: Both are standard measurements with a known result near 340 m/s.

check.stem: State the independent and dependent variables shared by the two speed-of-sound experiments.
check.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the distance the sound travels and the dependent variable is the time the sound takes to travel that distance.

check.stem: State the two quantities the oscilloscope method needs before a speed can be computed.
check.modelAnswer: The microphone separation (measured with the tape) and the pulse delay read from the screen.

check.stem: Explain why the microphone separation is kept small in the oscilloscope method.
check.modelAnswer: A short, precisely measured separation keeps the experiment compact on a bench and lets the oscilloscope display both pulses on one screen with a clear, readable offset, while the electronic timing keeps the error small despite the short travel time.

check.stem: The microphones are 2.0 m apart and the second pulse arrives 5.9 ms after the first. Calculate the speed of sound and compare it with the accepted value.
check.modelAnswer: Speed = 2.0 / 0.0059 = about 339 m/s, which is within about 1% of the accepted 340 m/s, so the result supports the accepted value.

glossary.definition: A rolling wheel of known circumference used to measure distances by counting rotations.
The delay between a person perceiving an event and responding to it, a source of random timing error.
The signal event that starts an oscilloscope drawing its trace, so every pulse is recorded from the same instant.
The smallest change an instrument can reliably display or record.
